title: “Pagod na ako”
note: Fictional patient and family. Survival figures are the module’s study results, not predictions for any one person, and no doses are given. Hospital policy on advance directives and the attending nephrologist guide every decision to withhold or withdraw dialysis.

monitor.family: Daughter at bedside; son in Riyadh

intro:
You are the nephrology resident on a medicine ward in Iloilo City. Mr. Teodoro “Lolo Teddy” Mangubat, 82, a retired fisherman, has been on hemodialysis for 18 months for diabetic kidney disease. He also has heart failure. This is his fourth admission in five months, each time with breathlessness, and he has lost weight. He now needs help to bathe and rarely leaves his bed between sessions. He is alert and oriented.

His daughter Ana, a public school teacher, cares for him at home. His son, Jun-Jun, works in Riyadh. This morning, as you finish examining him, Lolo Teddy holds your wrist and says quietly, “Pagod na ako, Doc. Ayoko na.”

choices.text: Reassure him that the next session will help, and that he will feel stronger once the fluid is off.
choices.feedback: Reassurance closes a door he has just opened. He may be telling you about symptoms, fear or a wish to stop, and you will not know unless you ask.
choices.then: You sit down, ask Lolo Teddy what he means and what is hardest, list his symptoms, and tell the attending nephrologist, Dr. Aquino, the same day. A family meeting is set for Thursday.

choices.text: Sit down, ask what he means, listen, and tell the attending the same day.
choices.feedback: Noticing and exploring suffering is real care. A patient who asks to stop dialysis is one of the module’s reasons to call the attending, and his words are the start of a goals-of-care conversation. Ask gently what is hardest for him, and report his words.

choices.text: Explain kindly that stopping dialysis is not allowed, because without it he would die.
choices.feedback: Stopping dialysis is ethically accepted when a patient with capacity decides its burdens outweigh its benefits. It is not suicide and not euthanasia. Telling him it is forbidden takes away a choice that is his.
choices.then: You sit down, ask Lolo Teddy what he means and what is hardest, list his symptoms, and tell the attending nephrologist, Dr. Aquino, the same day. A family meeting is set for Thursday.

n2.scene: Dr. Aquino, the attending, asks you to prepare for a family meeting on Thursday. You ask yourself the surprise question: would you be surprised if he died in the next year? The answer is no.
n2.prompt: How will you present his prognosis?

choices.text: Wait until he is clearly worse before raising prognosis, so the family is not frightened while he is stable.
choices.feedback: Waiting is gentle but costly. A “no” to the surprise question is a prompt to start the conversation now, while he can still take part.
choices.then: You and Dr. Aquino prepare ranges and scenarios instead: the best, most likely and worst course with dialysis and without, and what each would mean for his days.

vitals.prog: Ranges and scenarios, with and without dialysis

choices.text: Tell the family that, from the surprise question, he has less than a year to live.
choices.feedback: The surprise question identifies risk; it does not tell anyone when a person will die. In Moss’s study, 1-year mortality in the “no” group was 29.4%: seven of ten were still alive at a year.
choices.then: You and Dr. Aquino prepare ranges and scenarios instead: the best, most likely and worst course with dialysis and without, and what each would mean for his days.

vitals.prog: Ranges and scenarios, with and without dialysis

choices.text: Honest ranges and scenarios, with and without dialysis, in his own terms.
choices.feedback: Prognosis changes what people choose. His age, dependence, heart failure, weight loss and repeated admissions predict a short and difficult road, but the honest form of that is a range, with its uncertainty named. Best, most likely and worst course: time in hospital, time at home, what he can still do.

vitals.prog: Ranges and scenarios, with and without dialysis

n3.scene: Ana sits beside the bed. Jun-Jun joins by video from Riyadh and says at once, “Do everything. PhilHealth pays for the sessions anyway.” Lolo Teddy looks at the phone and says, “Bahala na ang mga anak ko.”
n3.prompt: How do you lead the meeting?

choices.text: Since Jun-Jun is paying for most of the care, let him and Ana decide together, and record that the family chose to continue.
choices.feedback: Lolo Teddy has capacity, so the decision is his, even if he chooses to share it. And dialysis must never be pressed on a frail patient because PhilHealth covers the sessions.
choices.then: You start again with a headline and a pause, then ask Lolo Teddy what matters most and how he wants the decision made. He says he wants to decide with his children, and what he wants them to choose is home.

vitals.plan: Stop dialysis; comfort-focused care at home

choices.text: Open with his latest laboratory results and dialysis adequacy, so the family understands the medical facts first.
choices.feedback: Numbers before a headline lose the room. REMAP starts with reframing (“the situation has changed”) and making space for emotion before facts.
choices.then: You start again with a headline and a pause, then ask Lolo Teddy what matters most and how he wants the decision made. He says he wants to decide with his children, and what he wants them to choose is home.

vitals.plan: Stop dialysis; comfort-focused care at home

choices.text: A headline, a pause, then what matters to him and how he wants to decide.
choices.feedback: This follows REMAP: Reframe, Expect emotion, Map out goals, Align, Propose. “Bahala na” may mean trust, or may hide a wish he does not want to burden them with. Asking what he would want them to choose keeps his values in the lead. Ask whether he wants to decide himself or with his children, and what he would want them to choose.

vitals.plan: Stop dialysis; comfort-focused care at home

choices.text: Propose a time-limited trial right away: continue dialysis for a set number of weeks, with written goals, and review on a date.
choices.feedback: A time-limited trial helps when the future is uncertain or a family is not ready. But you have not yet heard what he wants; map his goals before proposing a plan.
choices.then: You start again with a headline and a pause, then ask Lolo Teddy what matters most and how he wants the decision made. He says he wants to decide with his children, and what he wants them to choose is home.

vitals.plan: Stop dialysis; comfort-focused care at home

n4.scene: Lolo Teddy has chosen to stop dialysis and go home, and Ana agrees. At 23:30 Jun-Jun calls the ward and asks for you: “Doc, please. Schedule him for dialysis tomorrow. I will sign whatever you need.”

choices.text: Acknowledge his love, say his father’s decision stands, and call Dr. Aquino tonight.
choices.feedback: A relative abroad asking you to override the patient’s decision is on the module’s stop-and-call list. Distant children often carry guilt; give him the same information and respect, and return to his father’s words. Offer a call with Dr. Aquino in the morning, and document the conversation.

vitals.family: Jun-Jun informed and heard; decision stands

choices.text: Book a dialysis session for tomorrow morning to calm the family down, and let the day team sort it out.
choices.feedback: That overrides a capable patient’s decision at the request of someone who is not the decision-maker. It also hands the conflict to others instead of calling the attending.
choices.then: You call Dr. Aquino, who speaks with Jun-Jun the next morning. The decision Lolo Teddy made stands, and Jun-Jun’s worries are heard and written down.

vitals.family: Jun-Jun informed and heard; decision stands

choices.text: Tell him kindly that you cannot change the plan, and suggest he call the ward again in the morning.
choices.feedback: Holding the line is right, but he deserves to be heard. The attending should know tonight, and the call should be documented.
choices.then: You call Dr. Aquino, who speaks with Jun-Jun the next morning. The decision Lolo Teddy made stands, and Jun-Jun’s worries are heard and written down.

vitals.family: Jun-Jun informed and heard; decision stands

n5.scene: Dialysis has stopped. Ana asks, “Gaano pa po katagal, Doc? And what do we do at home?”

choices.text: Tell her honestly that nobody can say how long, and that the team will guide them day by day.
choices.feedback: Uncertainty is real, but refusing to estimate leaves the family unprepared. The evidence gives a useful range.
choices.then: Dr. Aquino and you meet the family again: usually about a week, sometimes days, occasionally several weeks; a symptom plan; burdensome tests and medicines stopped; and a home plan with a number to call.

vitals.plan: Home: comfort medicines, contact number, family taught

choices.text: Tell her that now dialysis has stopped, there is nothing more the hospital can do, so they should take him home.
choices.feedback: When dialysis stops, care does not. Breathlessness, agitation, twitching and pain each have a cause the team can treat for comfort.
choices.then: Dr. Aquino and you meet the family again: usually about a week, sometimes days, occasionally several weeks; a symptom plan; burdensome tests and medicines stopped; and a home plan with a number to call.

vitals.plan: Home: comfort medicines, contact number, family taught

choices.text: Usually about a week, sometimes less or more; then a comfort plan and a night number.
choices.feedback: In 1,947 hospice patients who stopped dialysis, mean survival was 7.4 days (range 0 to 40). Families need that range and a plan. Daily tests and medicines such as phosphate binders add burden without benefit now; the attending decides with the family and writes it down. Comfort medicines chosen for low kidney function, stopping burdensome tests and drugs, a family member taught to give the medicines.

vitals.plan: Home: comfort medicines, contact number, family taught

choices.text: Reassure her that he may have several months if he keeps eating well.
choices.feedback: That is not what the evidence shows, and false hope leaves the family unprepared for the next days.
choices.then: Dr. Aquino and you meet the family again: usually about a week, sometimes days, occasionally several weeks; a symptom plan; burdensome tests and medicines stopped; and a home plan with a number to call.

vitals.plan: Home: comfort medicines, contact number, family taught

end.title: Eight days later
end.text: Lolo Teddy died at home on the eighth day, drowsy and comfortable, with Ana and his grandchildren beside him and Jun-Jun on the phone during the prayers. The parish priest came on the second day. Ana called the team twice at night about breathlessness and was talked through the medicines each time. Your notes record his words, the options, his decision and whom he chose to decide with him.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • “Pagod na ako” is an opening. Explore it, list the symptoms, and tell the attending the same day.
  • The surprise question prompts a conversation, not a prediction. Give prognosis as ranges and scenarios, with and without dialysis.
  • Use REMAP, and ask the patient how he wants decisions made. His values lead, even when he shares the decision; coverage never decides for him.
  • A relative asking you to override the patient: listen, hold the decision, call the attending, document.
  • When dialysis stops, care continues: usually about a week (range 0 to 40 days), every symptom treated for comfort.

See Prognosis, The conversation and Withdrawal and end of life.
